summary: Singularis is a public, interactive viewer for real NASA SPHEREx observations. Users enter sky coordinates, retrieve multiple dated FITS cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA, inspect aligned frames, and play them as a time series. Each frame reports its observation time, wavelength, source data, and quality limits. A reproducible demonstration measures the motion of the known Epsilon Indi B system across three SPHEREx epochs: 6.49 ± 0.73 arcseconds, consistent with an independent 6.48 arcsecond catalog prediction. The result validates a method for inspecting sky changes; it is not a claim of a new object. The website, source code, and science audit are public so others can explore and review the evidence.
details:
Singularis turns repeated SPHEREx sky observations into an accessible visual time series. A visitor enters right ascension and declination. The Python service queries NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA2 for real SPHEREx exposures, retrieves FITS cutouts, validates masks and observation metadata, and selects observations from distinct dates. Astropy reads FITS headers, world coordinates, and times; reproject places frames on a common WCS grid; NumPy and Pillow prepare display images. The HTML, CSS, and JavaScript viewer presents frames, source FITS links, dates, wavelengths, animation, and quality information.

Our scientific demonstration uses three detector D6 observations of the known Epsilon Indi B field, dated 2025-04-29, 2025-06-10, and 2026-09-28, near 4.661 micrometers. After alignment, a Gaussian approximation to the effective point-spread function estimates the unresolved source position in each frame. The measured displacement between the first and last epochs is 6.49 ± 0.73 arcseconds. An independent Gaia-based proper-motion and parallax prediction is 6.48 arcseconds. The quoted 8.9 sigma is conditional on the stated uncertainty model. This validates known motion; it does not establish a new celestial discovery. Limits include one directly checked stationary reference source, unresolved Epsilon Indi Ba/Bb, and simplified PSF fitting.

The public website lets users inspect other coordinates and compare dated observations; it does not classify a source automatically or guarantee usable multi-epoch data for every field. The audit, reproducible results, and source code are at https://github.com/Isen7/Singularis . AI assistance was used for code, analysis workflow, and text drafting; the astronomical images come from the cited mission data.
dataRefs: NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx Data Explorer and FITS observations
projectRefs: ESA Gaia archive (proper motion and parallax comparison)
